final_note: You worked through Waves in air, fluids and solids: Transverse and longitudinal waves — 5 specification statements.

concepts.def: A travelling oscillation that carries energy from one place to another without the material it passes through being carried along. Waves may be either transverse or longitudinal.
A wave in which the oscillations are at right angles (perpendicular) to the direction in which the wave travels.
A wave in which the oscillations are along (parallel to) the direction in which the wave travels.
The standard example of a transverse wave. The surface of the water oscillates up and down while the ripple itself travels outwards across the surface, at right angles to that up-and-down movement.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are pushed closer together than normal, so the density and the pressure there are higher than normal.
A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are spread further apart than normal, so the density and the pressure there are lower than normal.
A longitudinal wave. A vibrating source such as a loudspeaker cone pushes and pulls the air next to it, sending a series of compressions and rarefactions travelling out through the air.
Each particle of the material vibrates to and fro about one position and returns to it. The particle does not travel along with the wave; it only passes the disturbance on to its neighbours.

concepts.term: Direction of travel of the wave
concepts.def: The direction in which the wave itself moves away from the source. A wave is classified as transverse or longitudinal by comparing the direction of the oscillations with this direction, not with 'up and down' or 'sideways'.

A cork or polystyrene ball floating in a ripple tank bobs up and down in the same place as ripples pass beneath it, instead of being carried to the far side. The ripple crosses the tank; the water does not.

A loudspeaker can be heard right across a room, yet no draught of air arrives with the sound and the air by the loudspeaker is never used up. The sound wave crosses the room; the air itself only vibrates in place.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the types of wave is correct?
options: All waves are transverse, as diagrams show.
The type depends on how the wave is drawn.
Water waves are the only transverse waves.
A wave is either transverse or longitudinal.
mcqs.explain: The specification states that waves may be either transverse or longitudinal; these are the two types.

mcqs.q: Ripples on a water surface are an example of which type of wave, and for what reason?
options: Longitudinal: the water is pushed outwards from where the stone landed.
Longitudinal: each bit of water travels along with the ripple it is in.
Transverse: the surface moves up and down as the ripple moves outwards.
Transverse: the ripples spread out in circles across the whole surface.
mcqs.explain: The oscillation of the surface is at right angles to the direction the ripple travels, which is what makes a wave transverse.

mcqs.q: A small polystyrene ball floats in a ripple tank while straight ripples pass beneath it. What does the ball do?
options: It is carried along with the ripples to the far end of the tank.
It bobs up and down in the same place as each ripple passes.
It moves back and forth along the direction the ripples travel.
It stays completely still because the ripples pass underneath it.
mcqs.explain: The surface oscillates vertically about a fixed position, so the ball rises and falls without moving along.

mcqs.q: In a sound wave travelling through air, what is a compression?
options: A region where the air particles are pushed closer together.
A region where the air particles are squashed into a smaller size.
A region where the air particles are held still by the pressure.
A region where all the air particles move in the same direction.
mcqs.explain: A compression is a region of higher density and pressure, produced by the particles being crowded together.

mcqs.q: What is a rarefaction in a sound wave travelling through air?
options: A region of totally empty space with no air particles inside it.
A region where the air particles have stopped vibrating for now.
A region where the air particles are further apart than normal.
A region where the air particles have expanded to a larger size.
mcqs.explain: A rarefaction is a region of lower density and pressure, with the particles more spread out.

mcqs.q: A loudspeaker cone moves forwards and backwards. What does this produce in the air in front of it?
options: A stream of air pushed out from the cone towards the listener.
Compressions and rarefactions travelling outwards through the air.
Side-to-side ripples in the air, like ripples on a water surface.
Compressions only, with undisturbed air in the gaps between.
mcqs.explain: A longitudinal sound wave shows areas of compression and rarefaction, sent out as the cone pushes and pulls the air.

mcqs.q: How do the density and pressure of the air compare in a compression and in a rarefaction?
options: Both are higher in a compression and lower in a rarefaction.
Both stay the same, since only the spacing of particles changes.
Air pressure is higher in a compression; a rarefaction has none.
Density is unchanged because the particles change in size only.
mcqs.explain: Crowding the particles together raises the density and pressure; spreading them apart lowers both.

mcqs.q: In a transverse wave, how do the oscillations compare with the direction the wave travels?
options: They are always up and down, whichever way the wave goes.
They are at right angles to the direction the wave travels.
They are along the direction the wave travels, as in sound.
They are in a circle around the direction the wave travels.
mcqs.explain: This is the defining property of a transverse wave: oscillation perpendicular to the direction of travel.

mcqs.q: A rope hangs down from a hook. A student shakes the bottom end from side to side and a wave travels up the rope. Which type of wave is it?
options: Transverse, because the oscillation is at right angles to the travel.
Longitudinal, because the movement is sideways here, not up and down.
Longitudinal, because the wave travels along the length of the rope.
Transverse, because a rope is only ever able to carry that type.
mcqs.explain: The rope moves horizontally while the wave moves vertically, so the two directions are perpendicular.

mcqs.q: A slinky lying on a bench is pushed and pulled along its own length. Which description of the wave that travels along it is correct?
options: Coils travel from one end of the slinky to the other with the wave.
Coils vibrate up and down, so this must be a transverse wave instead.
Coils vibrate along the slinky, making compressions and rarefactions.
Coils stay still while compressions move along the slinky past them.
mcqs.explain: The oscillation is parallel to the direction of travel, which is what produces the areas of compression and rarefaction.

mcqs.q: Which of these is evidence that it is the sound wave, and not the air, that crosses a room?
options: A loudspeaker blows dust off its cone when the volume is high.
Each air particle travels from the loudspeaker to the listener.
Turning the volume up makes the loudspeaker cone move further.
You can hear a distant loudspeaker with no draught reaching you.
mcqs.explain: Air arriving from the loudspeaker would be felt as a wind; the sound arrives and the air does not.

mcqs.q: Ripples cross a pond and reach the far bank. What does this tell you about the water in the pond?
options: The water at the near bank has moved across to the far bank now.
The water moves across the pond at the same speed as the ripple.
The water level at the far bank rises for good as ripples arrive.
Each part of the surface moves up and down as the ripple goes by.
mcqs.explain: The disturbance is passed on from one part of the surface to the next, so each part only oscillates in place.

mcqs.q: Suppose the air really did travel along with a sound wave. What would a listener notice?
options: Nothing new at all, because sound already is a movement of air.
Each particle vibrating about a fixed point, just as it does now.
Every sound getting steadily louder as it moved from the source.
A wind blowing out from the source whenever a sound was made.
mcqs.explain: Air moving from source to listener is a flow of air, which is exactly what a wind is; no such wind is observed.

mcqs.q: Sound travelling through air is compared with ripples on a water surface. Which statement is correct?
options: Sound oscillates along its direction of travel; ripples oscillate across it.
Both are transverse waves, because both can be drawn as a wavy curve.
Both are longitudinal waves, because both spread outwards from a source.
Ripples oscillate along their travel; sound oscillates across its travel.
mcqs.explain: Sound in air is longitudinal and ripples on water are transverse, which is precisely this difference.
